brand.name: Patagonia
brand.tagline: MADE FOR THE MOMENT. BUILT FOR A LIFETIME.
brand.elevatorPitch: We make outdoor gear for the moments you chase—first chair, fresh trails and far-flung summits. We use our business, voice and resources to build power in the grassroots environmental movement and protect the wild places our community depends on.
brand.boilerplate: About Patagonia: Patagonia is a U.S.-based outdoor apparel company with a 50-year history of environmental activism. Since 1985, it has used its business, voice and resources to support the grassroots environmental movement. Through Patagonia Action Works, it connects individuals with nonprofit partners, while its self-imposed Earth tax, 1% for the Planet, supports environmental nonprofits around the globe.
brand.description: Patagonia is a designer of outdoor clothing and gear for the silent sports: climbing, surfing, skiing and snowboarding, fly fishing, and trail running

voice.summary: Action-led and collectively minded, pairing vivid outdoor language with direct environmental commitments and detailed, evidence-based advocacy.

traits.name: Business as Activism
traits.description: Treats environmental action as a core business responsibility, not a peripheral cause.
traits.do: Name the action Patagonia takes and the environmental interests it serves.
traits.dont: Substitute vague statements about caring for concrete commitments.

traits.name: Collective and Mobilizing
traits.description: Uses shared responsibility and practical invitations to move people toward participation.
traits.do: Use we and our to frame shared stakes, then offer a specific way to participate.
traits.dont: Leave readers with an abstract problem and no next step.

evidence.quote: But as threats to our home planet grow, so does the need for collective action.

traits.name: Outdoor-Specific and Evocative
traits.description: Grounds product language in recognizable outdoor experiences rather than generic lifestyle aspiration.
traits.do: Use concrete terrain, activities and moments to describe what gear enables.
traits.dont: Rely on luxury language or empty claims about adventure.

evidence.quote: Our Winter ’26 New Arrivals are made for the moments you chase—first chair, fresh trails and far-flung summits.
It’s gear that meets you in the moment and helps keep you there.

traits.name: Firm, Evidence-Led Advocacy
traits.description: States a clear position and supports it with policy detail, economic stakes and quantified evidence.
traits.do: Pair policy positions with named rules, specific consequences and relevant numbers.
traits.dont: Replace reasoned opposition with insults or unsupported certainty.

evidence.quote: We write in strong opposition to the U.S. Department of Agriculture's (USDA) proposal to rescind the 2001 Roadless Rule.
A February 2026 national poll found 76 percent of likely voters support keeping the Roadless Rule intact.[3]

styleRules: Use Title Case for most headings; reserve all caps for a short campaign statement like the home-page slogan.
Aim for sentences around 19 words, allowing longer, information-dense sentences in policy advocacy.
Favor first-person plural for commitments and shared responsibility; use second person selectively for gear and participation.
Use declarative sentences and direct imperatives, without exclamation marks or rhetorical questions.
Use contractions in consumer and activism copy; adopt more formal phrasing in official policy correspondence.
Preserve precise figures, dates and policy names; expand technical acronyms on first mention in advocacy copy.

audiences.name: Outdoor recreationists
audiences.need: Gear for skiing, trails and summits, alongside protection of the wild places their recreation depends on.

audiences.name: Environmental advocates and volunteers
audiences.need: Ways to connect with environmental groups through events, petitions, skilled volunteering and donations.

audiences.name: Environmental nonprofits
audiences.need: Funding, community participation and support for protecting air, land and water.

audiences.name: Policymakers and outdoor-economy communities
audiences.need: Evidence connecting conservation with livelihoods, public support and long-term economic stability.

pillars.headline: Gear for the Moment, Built for a Lifetime
pillars.message: Patagonia presents outdoor gear as made for specific experiences and built for lasting use.

proof.quote: MADE FOR THE MOMENT. BUILT FOR A LIFETIME.
It’s gear that meets you in the moment and helps keep you there.

pillars.headline: Business Powers Environmental Action
pillars.message: Patagonia puts business resources and self-imposed funding behind grassroots environmental protection.

proof.quote: Since 1985, we’ve used our business, voice and resources to build power in the grassroots environmental movement.
Patagonia’s self-imposed Earth tax, 1% for the Planet, provides support to environmental nonprofits working to defend our air, land and water around the globe.

pillars.headline: Collective Action Starts with Participation
pillars.message: Patagonia invites individuals to join environmental groups and take practical action on urgent issues.

proof.quote: We’re connecting individuals with Patagonia grantees, to take action on the most pressing issues facing the world today.
11.2M environmental voters skipped the last election. Together, we can change that.

pillars.headline: Healthy Wild Places Sustain Livelihoods
pillars.message: Protecting wild places supports Patagonia’s business, outdoor recreation and the communities that depend on them.

proof.quote: The future of our business, the outdoor recreation economy and our planet relies on the health of wild places, including inventoried roadless areas.
That certainty has helped businesses like ours invest in gateway communities and build lasting partnerships.

proofPoints.quote: Patagonia is a U.S.-based outdoor apparel company with a 50-year history of environmental activism.
Since 1985, we’ve used our business, voice and resources to build power in the grassroots environmental movement.
Patagonia’s self-imposed Earth tax, 1% for the Planet, provides support to environmental nonprofits working to defend our air, land and water around the globe.
Recreation on public lands, much of it centered on backcountry experiences, anchors a $1.3 trillion national outdoor recreation economy that supports 5.2 million American jobs.
A February 2026 national poll found 76 percent of likely voters support keeping the Roadless Rule intact.[3]
